Where it began

Rahul Dravid was born in Indore on 11 January 1973, and grew up in Bangalore after his family moved there. He took up the game at 12, and the former cricketer Keki Tarapore noticed his talent at a summer camp at the Chinnaswamy Stadium. He came through the Karnataka age-group sides, and in those days he kept wicket as well as batting.

He was a good student too, with a commerce degree from St Joseph's, and he was working towards an MBA when India picked him. His first Ranji Trophy match came in February 1991, before he had finished college, and he scored 82 in it.

The player

His Test debut came at Lord's on 20 June 1996. Batting at seven, alongside a fellow debutant called Sourav Ganguly, he made 95. There would be many hundreds later: 36 of them in 164 Tests, among 13,288 runs at 52.31, with a best of 270. By October 2026 only four men had made more Test runs.

Two partnerships with V. V. S. Laxman stand out. At Eden Gardens in 2001, India followed on against Australia and then won, after the pair added 376. At Adelaide in the 2003–04 series they put on 303 and Dravid went on to 233. He also held 210 catches in the field, and he captained India in 25 Tests.

What made him special

His technique was the thing. He could bat for hours, and he finished with more balls faced and more time at the crease than anyone in Test history. He became the first man to score a Test hundred in each of the ten Test-playing countries of his time. No wonder he was called The Wall and Mr Dependable.

The one-day game took him longer to crack. Early on he was labelled a Test specialist, so he widened his range of strokes and learned to pace an innings. It worked: he was the leading run-scorer at the 1999 World Cup and later kept wicket for India in one-day cricket, including at the 2003 World Cup.

Away from the middle

Wisden made him a Cricketer of the Year in 2000, and in 2004 he was named Player of the Year at the first ICC awards. In 2011 he became the first cricketer from outside Australia to give the Bradman Oration in Canberra, and in 2018 he entered the ICC Hall of Fame. He speaks Marathi, Kannada, English and Hindi.

After playing he turned to coaching. He led India's Under-19 side to the 2018 Under-19 World Cup, and as head coach of the senior team he guided India to the 2024 Twenty20 World Cup.

And finally

For all those runs, his Test bowling brought him a single wicket, Ridley Jacobs in the West Indies in 2002. Across his whole career that wicket cost him 39 runs, a price many full-time bowlers would happily have paid.
